utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-05-87-A, the Prosecutor versus Nikola Sainovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I now please have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Appearing today for the Prosecution, my name is Najwa Nabti, together with Laurel Baig and our Case Manager Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. My name is Toma Fila, attorney at law, and I am Defence counsel for Nikola Sainovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Tomislav Visnjic, Defence counsel for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Aleksandar Aleksic for the Defence of General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of General Lazarevic Defence team, myself, Djuro Cepic, as Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Attorney Dan Ivetic appearing on behalf of Sreten Lukic's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, could all the parties hear the proceedings in a language that they could understand? Mr. Sainovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand? THE APPELLANT SAINOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ojdanic? THE APPELLANT OJDANIC: [Interpretation] I am hearing you, yes, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic? THE APPELLANT PAVKOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic? THE APPELLANT LAZAREVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic? THE APPELLANT LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there's any problem that you could not follow the proceedings, do please let me know without any hesitation. This Status Conference is called in accordance with the Rule 65 bis B of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal which requires a Status Conference to be convened every 120 days during the appeal proceedings to allow any person in custody, pending appeal, the opportunity to raise issue in relation hereto, including the mental and the physical condition of that person. In the present case, the last Status Conference was held on the 14th September, 2010. For reasons of effective court management, this Status Conference was scheduled six days after the expiration of the 120-day period, following consultations with all the parties. Today's Status Conference was scheduled by the order issued on the 30th November, 2010. First I would like to inquire into the status of the detention conditions and the health situation of Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Ojdanic, Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Lukic. If you have any concern in relation to the detention condition or your state of health that cannot be resolved through the standard procedures, I would invite you to raise them now. If you wish, this discussion can take place in private session. Thank you. Yes, please, Mr. Pavkovic. THE APPELLANT PAVKOVIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in a few sentences I would like to inform you of my health conditions, since before the Status Conference that was held on the 14th of September there were quite a few discussions on this issue. On the 8th of December, my dental implants were fitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. As I said, that if you need the private session, we could have this discussion conducted in the private session. THE APPELLANT PAVKOVIC: [Interpretation] No, there is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed. THE APPELLANT PAVKOVIC: [Interpretation] I only want to briefly let you know that it was on the 8th of December that the surgery was conducted in the UNDU and both implants were fitted within an hour. This differed greatly from what I was told by the doctor on the 1st of June that the whole treatment would take six months, that the bone, the jaw bone, would have had to be operated on, et cetera. But the surgery went fine, and there is only some physical pain that I'm still suffering. I would like to let you know that when you were deciding on my motion for provisional release, you were furnished imprecise and inaccurate information about my health condition. And I'm letting you know this in order to make sure that such practice does not continue in the future. On the 13th of September, 2010, you received information from our service that it was down to me that the implants had not been fitted by then, which would have been the case, simply because I wanted to have the implants fitted in Serbia. This is not true, and my lawyers intervened. And Dr. Pavke [phoen], who is the doctor of the UNDU, said that the report was inaccurate and that a new report would follow. But it was only on the 20th of September that this report was made, and it stated that nothing had been done in the mean time to have the implants fitted simply because of the fact that I had filed my motion for provisional release. This was not true either, because I filed my motion for provisional release only on the 18th of November. In a subsequent report sent to you on the 26th of October, it was confirmed that the treatment should have started on the 29th of September but that it had not because I had refused to do so. Again there was misunderstanding there, because the original report by the implantologist reached you as part of the package of the material underlying the motion for provisional release. I would like to say that it has been the practice so far to send inaccurate reports about my health condition. I don't know what the case is with others, but I do know that I do not receive reports on the findings of my medical examinations in due time nor do I receive any other relevant material. What I do receive is written on a simple sheet of paper, which doesn't even have the letter heading of the doctor, and I'm sure this is not the proper way to go about it. As far as my health is concerned, new problems have emerged. According to a decision issued by the UNDU medical service, a dentist would be taking up his new position only in three weeks' time, so there is no control. Dr. Katan [phoen], and she's the lady doctor who was working on this so far, and she said that the -- the implants or the dentures should be fitted on the right side of my denture but that she lacked materials for it and she wasn't aware of when the materials would arrive. Now, the second issue, which is much more important to me, has to do with the judgement that I received in my own language. Since I have many problems in communicating with my lawyers on this issue, let me inform you of the following: I've reviewed the judgement carefully, and I came to realise that a great many documents that we had adduced as Defence had been imprecisely or inaccurately interpreted and therefore erroneous conclusions were drawn on their basis, or some of these documents that favoured Defence had not been taken into consideration at all. I've had difficulties with my lawyers in deciding as to how to include these objections that I would like to make in relation to documents into our appeal brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I certainly will convey your complaint to the Registry and to see what should be done concerning your state of health. As for the second issue, I believe that later on we still have the opportunity to discuss this matter with your counsel, and I thank you very much to bring your matter of concern to me. Well, is there any other matters that any party would like to bring concerning to his health? Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, you have the floor, please. THE APPELLANT LAZAREVIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for giving me, yet again, an opportunity to inform you briefly about my health in between two Status Conferences. Under a month and a half ago I underwent surgery for the seventh time in less than two years. I would, if you allow me, be cynical at my own expense and say that I was operated on because of an illness that I invented or exaggerated or something of the sort, because this is the sort of qualifications that were raised when my Defence or I informed you of the state of my health at Status Conferences. The situation is far more serious. And, of course, this is not an invented malaise, rather it was a rather urgent and critical ailment of the urinary tract. As you will recall, for the earlier surgery of the thrombosis of my right leg I resorted to a hunger strike in order to speed up the surgery and avert negative consequences. Again, doctors from the Royal Bronovo Hospital scheduled the operations to take one after another in the course of two days. So this was not a new illness that appeared out of the blue, and that's what I'd like to inform you about. This illness was diagnosed back in June of 2009, when I was undergoing a surgery in Serbia by a specialist, a doctor in medical science. My therapy was laid down, and the diagnosis was translated into English. The treatment began, but unfortunately I could not remain in Serbia at the time for longer than five days. I took the necessary medication and reported to the UNDU. I handed over my diagnosis and medication to the medical staff of the UNDU infirmary. Unfortunately for me, the medication was thrown away, the diagnosis was ignored, and you and your Chamber were informed in writing by the UNDU doctor that he had chosen to ignore some of the diagnoses rendered by other doctors. In the meantime, the illness progressed and reached its final stage where it compromised the entire urinary tract. At my written request addressed to the doctor to be admitted into a hospital, I was finally hospitalised at the very last moment, when no other remedy could be resorted to than an operation. Mr. President, I do not wish at this time to speculate what might have happened had the initially envisaged treatment been undertaken and whether the operation might have been avoided or not. I do not wish to say that this was the result of anyone's deliberate conduct either. Still, I don't think it's good to turn our eyes away from the bare fact and the truth of the matter which is that what was done and that, i.e., absence of treatment, in my case, was a departure from medical ethics and discipline, or as the president of the Tribunal President Robinson said, a violation of my human rights. Everybody knows who failed in their duty, and this was a flagrant case of lack of responsibility. I hope that in other quarters, in proper quarters, a discussion on this issue will be initiated in order to ascertain whose responsibility it ultimately was. What I would like to make sure in the courtroom is that it be fully clear that whatever I said and whatever my Defence said on my behalf was true, backed by arguments, and borne out to be true by the last two operations. From what I could tell, you received a report, and I received one too but only just before I entered the courtroom, which informed you that the operation had gone well. However, the post-operative treatment is a long-lasting one and not even the doctor who performed the surgery is able to ascertain to what extent I will be suffering from disability of my urinary tract. Speaking about this particular issue, Mr. President, please don't hold it against me what I'm going to say. I am a detainee who has undergone the largest number of surgeries and it has become inappropriate to request our Defence teams to prove what the benefits and advantages are of treatment in our home countries as opposed to that available in the Netherlands. These are basic things. I've informed, about this, the Appeals Chamber, the Registry, the president of the Court on the 28th of March. Allow me only to mention three minor examples, and I underline that those were insignificant examples because my dignity does not allow me to speak about more serious matters. I was operated on in a very expensive and reputable royal hospital, and due to that, they kept me only for two days after the surgery. However, the treatment I received during those two days was so expedited in terms of IV drip and other things which meant that in 24 hours I had to receive 30 or 40 litres of IV drip, which caused excruciating pain. I begged the medical staff to reduce the speed of the drip or to give me a shot of morphine in order for me to sustain the pain; however, this is expensive. And for the Tribunal not to pay these costs, they decided to transfer me to the Detention Unit hospital. This is simply unbearable and intolerable. Such kind of IV drip should take at least five or six days. Another example, which is also a minor one but nevertheless self-explanatory. As soon as I was put in a room in the hospital, they switched off the TV because nobody accepted to cover the costs. Of course, it's not the patient who can afford to pay that. This might be something funny, but I think that this is a regrettable approach because this is a cynical kind of treatment of the patient who requires a certain care. And thirdly, at my request, I was transferred from the detention hospital to my own detention cell. And in this cell, the nurses allegedly trained me to inject myself with the hypodermic syringe, and allegedly this is what I did for 25 days. How I did that and what I did, only I can tell; I'm not going to discuss this any further. I'd better stick to the saying of the former US President Johnson, which says that silent treatment is the strongest reprimand. Now, that's the first question. The next question, Mr. President, is the following: You know that the esteemed president of the Tribunal, Mr. Robinson, ever since April of last year has been trying to offer me the required assistance because his estimation was that my human rights were being violated. Despite the fact that he received a variety of reports from medical personnel that claimed otherwise, he said that that was not correct. Last year, in June and July, the administration, not the president himself, engaged a general practitioner with eight years of experience as a kind of medical expert, and, of course, this man was incapable of fulfilling any requests made by the Tribunal president. He even asked me what he was supposed to do. This expert report, if we may call it that, was written on one and a half pages only. Then some other bodies within the Tribunal who have nothing to do whatsoever with my medical treatment, by abiding to what this so-called expert wrote, gave their opinion. The Tribunal president was extremely dissatisfied with what he received. He asked me to put something on paper. I thanked him for his help and asked him to tell everybody to just forget about me altogether and not render any assistance to me. However, the president insisted and I had to comply and write the entire history of what had happened. The Tribunal president had three medical reports on his desk similar to the ones mentioned by General Pavkovic, full of inaccuracies, not supported by any documents, and I will really try to refrain from using any harsher words. The Tribunal president simply decided that his orders had not been fulfilled; that this so-called expert, even if he had wanted to carry out this task, he wouldn't have been able to do so because he was a mere general practitioner. Therefore, in October, he ordered the administration to find a new medical expert. Now a professor from Belgium, from Brussels, came who specialises in some kind of surgery or of some other branch of medicine. He did something, he left some things undone, though. And I'm telling you all this so that you would allow me to ask myself out loud in front of everybody present here: If over a period of one year the president of the Tribunal is unable to help me, how can I help myself with the medical officer that we have in the Detention Unit? The only recourse that I have, by relying on your patience and understanding, to complain to you and after that wait for Godot in my detention cell and wait for what the new day will bring to me. The third matter. This issue was prompted by this document that I received just as I was entering the courtroom. It relates to Dr. Eekhof's report, a medical officer from the Detention Unit infirmary, in which he said that I am more or less in a good condition. I suffered from paralysis attacks, and that happened even today, which he described as migraine attacks. In 2008, when this doctor as a Trial Chamber medical expert described my health condition, he detected serious problems and lesions in the left hemisphere of my brain. He even told me about the existence of these problems, but now he's calling it a migraine. Now, I needn't say more about the reports submitted by one in the same physician. Now, the fourth issue is something that causes me concern and embarrassment, but I would like to say, quite openly and candidly, that due to all these problems, numerous surgeries, suffering pain, humiliation, struggling with the windmills, means that I tried to prove that there is something rotten in the land of Denmark, it all proves that something is wrong with the system itself. I think that I have exhausted all my mental and physical capacities; my batteries are empty. In a nutshell, I find it very hard to tolerate and endure all the things happening recently. Yesterday, for example, I collapsed, lost consciousness. Today I had a paralysis attack. And all these things are happening day in and day out, and I'm still staying in my cell totally helpless, although you are receiving reports that everything is under control. For that reason I tasked my Defence team to approach you and the Appeals Chamber with the request for leave for a short recuperation period which I would spend at home. I believe that that would contribute to the improvement of my health condition and my speedy recovery. And eventually it will contribute to the capacity for me to continue enduring these proceedings, already announced of surgeries on my both knees, and it seems that I will have to use crutches, which will make me a first-category disabled person. I know that everything is in your hands, that we depend on your mercy, but, nevertheless, I would like to thank you in advance for your understanding and patience which you demonstrated today, once again. And for that I am extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. I take note of your submissions. But first, as I have recalled on several occasions, according to the Rule 80 and 81 of the detention rules, where a detainee is not satisfied with the conditions of his or her detention, he or she is entitled to make a complaint to the commanding officer or his representative at any time. And in case of a unsatisfactory response, to make a written complaint, without censorship, to the Registrar, who shall inform the President. This is the right procedure that you have to follow. Secondly, I can assure you I myself took whatever you and your counsel submitted very seriously. I have done my best to help you concerning with your state of health. Suchly, I would like to share me own experience with you concerning with the medical treatment. I believe that whenever you are hospitalised, you are entirely in the hands of the doctors, because they are specially trained experts. As a judge, I am not in the position to comment on what kind of treatment is appropriate. I think this is the three points I would like to mention to you on this very issue. Well, it seems to me that we have exhausted the subject on this -- on this subject. Before we turn to any issues that the parties may wish to raise, I would like to briefly mention a few outstanding matters. There are currently two pending motions before the Appeals Chamber. Both motions were filed in response to the translation of the Trial Judgement into B/C/S which was issued on the 13th September, 2010. The first motion was filed on the 17th December, 2010 by counsel for Mr. Lukic, seeking to vary his appeal. It is now fully briefed, and a decision will be issued by the Appeals Chamber in due course. The second pending motion was filed confidentially by counsel for Mr. Sainovic on the 11th January, 2011, seeking leave to vary his appeal and admit additional evidence pursuant to Rule 115 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The briefing is not yet complete. The motion will be considered and determined by the Appeals Chamber in due course. In this context, I note that counsel for Mr. Ojdanic filed a submission on 13th December, 2010, informing the Appeals Chamber that Mr. Ojdanic does not seek to further vary the grounds of his appeal. Recalling that at a Status Conference of the 14th September, 2010, the Defence was strongly encouraged to seek leave to vary their grounds of appeal as soon as possible so that their motions may be decided upon and a supplemental briefing completed, where applicable, before the end of the year. I believe that Mr. Pavkovic has mentioned that in his submissions. Now I would like to give the floor to the counsel for Mr. Pavkovic to explain to me on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. What our client wanted to say was that the notes he made, in which I reviewed carefully, covered some 250 pages, and they were, of course, made in relation to the Trial Judgement translation in the B/C/S. I've been translating these notes for Mr. Ackerman, who is in the United States, he isn't here, and we are working on this, but the procedure has not been yet completed. So we will be asking leave to amend and supplement our appeals brief, and that's what Mr. Pavkovic referred to. I have nothing else to add on this score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please give me a approximate time that you will file your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to consult with my learned friend Mr. Ackerman, but we will do our best to do this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any more submissions on this matter? It seems to me there's none. At this point I would like to ask parties whether they have any other issues that they would like to raise at this time. Is there any issue the Prosecution would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'm turning to the counsel for Mr. Sainovic. Do you have any other issues you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you very much. Or I'd like to inform you that I decided that the motion should not be made confidential after all, so it will go through the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And the counsel for Mr. Ojdanic, do you have any other issues you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel for Mr. Pavkovic, do you have any other issues to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Nothing to raise, Your Honour. Nothing to raise. Our client raised clear position regarding to the medical treatment, so we have got nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Lukic, do you have any other issues you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have nothing at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, this concludes today's Status Conference. I thank the parties for their attendance and adjourn this proceedings.
